lead: You will learn how IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are written, split and grouped. You will read an IP datagram, fragment it, and follow a packet through ARP, ICMP, DHCP and NAT. You will then compare RIP, OSPF and BGP and compute shortest paths by hand.
about: This unit is the network layer's addressing and routing core. Chapter 4.1 starts with 32-bit IPv4 addresses and the shift from classful to classless prefixes. Chapter 4.2 turns prefixes into subnets and CIDR blocks. Chapter 4.3 reads the IPv4 header and fragments a datagram to fit an MTU. Chapter 4.4 moves to 128-bit IPv6 and its transition. Chapter 4.5 covers the helpers ARP, ICMP, DHCP and NAT. Chapter 4.6 separates static and dynamic, flat and hierarchical routing. Chapters 4.7, 4.8 and 4.9 build distance vector/RIP, link state/OSPF and path vector/BGP in that order. Each chapter gives one worked numerical example and one exam trap.

chapters.idea: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit identifier split into a network part and a host part; classful addressing fixes that split by first-octet range, while classless addressing writes the split as a /n prefix.
chapters.depth: Cover dotted-decimal notation, 32-bit binary view, classes A–E, default masks /8, /16 and /24, network address, directed broadcast, first and last usable host, private ranges and special addresses. Explain classless prefixes and CIDR notation as the modern replacement; introduce longest prefix match only as the lookup rule that 4.2 expands. Some syllabi call classful addressing legacy addressing and classless addressing CIDR. Keep historical class D and E brief.

figure.title: One address, two readings
figure.aria: The address 172.16.5.10 with mask 255.255.252.0 gives network 172.16.4.0, broadcast 172.16.7.255 and usable hosts .4.1 to .7.254; the classful class B default is /16.

chapters.example: For 172.16.5.10/22, give the network address, broadcast address, usable host range, and its classful class with default mask. Answer: mask 255.255.252.0; network 172.16.4.0; broadcast 172.16.7.255; hosts 172.16.4.1 to 172.16.7.254; class B, default /16.
chapters.trap: Using the classful default mask when a /n is written, and forgetting that the network and broadcast addresses are not usable hosts.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: TCP/IP layering; binary numbers and powers of two.
chapters.leave: Subnetting and CIDR aggregation to 4.2; fragmentation to 4.3; NAT to 4.5.

chapters.idea: Subnetting borrows host bits to make smaller networks inside a prefix, and CIDR/VLSM let different prefixes have different lengths so addresses fit real host counts.
chapters.depth: Cover subnet masks, subnet address, directed broadcast, usable hosts, 2^s subnets and 2^h − 2 hosts. Work VLSM by allocating the largest requirement first. Explain CIDR aggregation, route summarisation and longest prefix match. Some syllabi call VLSM variable length subnet mask networks. Keep routing protocol details out; only show that a router stores prefixes.

figure.aria: The /24 block 192.168.1.0 is split by VLSM into /25 for 100 hosts, /26 for 50, /27 for 25 and /28 for 10, leaving 240–255 unused.

chapters.trap: Allocating the small subnet first so the large subnet has no aligned block, and forgetting that /27 gives 30 usable hosts, not 32.

chapters.idea: The IPv4 datagram has a fixed header plus options; when its size exceeds the link MTU, it is fragmented and reassembled using identification, flags and a fragment offset counted in 8-byte units.
chapters.depth: Cover header fields: version, IHL, DSCP/ECN, total length, identification, flags DF/MF, fragment offset, TTL, protocol, header checksum, source and destination, options. Explain MTU, fragmentation, reassembly and path MTU discovery (added: it completes the subject). Some syllabi call the datagram a packet. Keep TCP segmentation out.

figure.title: Fragments for MTU 1500
figure.aria: A 3980-byte payload is cut into data sizes 1480, 1480 and 1020 bytes; offsets are 0, 185 and 370 in 8-byte units, with MF flags 1, 1, 0.

chapters.example: An IPv4 datagram is 4000 bytes, including a 20-byte header, so its data is 3980 bytes. It crosses a link with MTU 1500 bytes. Give each fragment's data size, total length, offset and MF flag. Answer: data 1480, 1480, 1020; total lengths 1500, 1500, 1040; offsets 0, 185, 370; MF 1, 1, 0.
chapters.trap: Fragment offset counts 8-byte blocks, not bytes; the last fragment's data length need not be a multiple of 8.
chapters.leave: TCP segmentation to Unit 5; IPv6 header changes to 4.4.

chapters.idea: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a fixed 40-byte base header; transition from IPv4 uses dual stack, tunnelling and translation.
chapters.depth: Cover eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, :: compression once, address types unicast, multicast and anycast, /64 LAN prefixes and SLAAC as flexible addressing. Compare the IPv6 header with IPv4: no header checksum, routers do not fragment, extension headers, hop limit replaces TTL. Cover dual stack, tunnelling and translation at overview level. Some syllabi call this IPv6 transition.

figure.aria: The fixed IPv6 header carries version, traffic class, flow label, payload length, next header, hop limit, then 128-bit source and destination addresses.

chapters.example: Expand and compress 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329. Give the /64 LAN prefix and one transition method. Answer: compressed 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329; /64 prefix 2001:db8:0:0::/64; transition by dual stack.
chapters.trap: Using :: twice in one address, treating the IPv6 header as variable length, and forgetting that hop limit replaces TTL.
chapters.leave: IPv6 routing protocol details to 4.8; NAT64 details to 4.5.

chapters.idea: ARP finds a MAC address for an IP address on a LAN, ICMP reports errors and queries, DHCP assigns addresses, and NAT shares public addresses across private hosts.
chapters.depth: Cover ARP request, reply and cache; mention RARP as obsolete (advanced: only a few universities still list it). Cover ICMP error and query messages, ping and traceroute. Cover DHCP DORA and relay. Cover NAT and PAT tables, private ranges and limitations such as broken end-to-end reachability. Some syllabi call PAT NAPT.

figure.aria: The host ARPs for its gateway, gets MAC aa:bb, sends a packet from 192.168.1.10:4000, and the router NATs the source to 203.0.113.5:4000.

chapters.example: Host 192.168.1.10 (MAC 00:11) has DHCP lease with gateway 192.168.1.1 (MAC aa:bb) and sends to 8.8.8.8:80 from port 4000. The router's public address is 203.0.113.5. Show the ARP messages and the NAT table entry. Answer: ARP request asks who has 192.168.1.1; reply gives aa:bb; NAT maps 192.168.1.10:4000 to 203.0.113.5:4000.
chapters.trap: ARP resolves IP to MAC, not names; NAT translates addresses and ports, not application data.
chapters.leave: DNS to Unit 6; TCP/UDP port details to Unit 5; security to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Routing chooses paths and builds tables; static routes are manual, dynamic protocols learn, and hierarchical routing keeps large tables small.
chapters.depth: Cover routing versus forwarding, control plane versus data plane, static versus dynamic, flat versus hierarchical, host-based versus router-intelligent (advanced: only a few universities teach this), centralized versus distributed, and routing metrics. Explain autonomous systems, areas and route summarisation. Keep RIP, OSPF and BGP algorithms for later chapters.

figure.aria: Four /24 networks 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.3.0 are summarised by one /22 route 10.0.0.0/22 at the core.

chapters.example: Aggregate 10.0.0.0/24, 10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24 and 10.0.3.0/24. How many entries does a flat table need, and how many at a hierarchical core? Answer: flat table has 4 entries; core uses one summary 10.0.0.0/22, with the four /24 entries at the edge.
chapters.trap: Thinking a summary route overrides more specific prefixes; longest prefix match still selects the /24 when present.
chapters.leave: RIP, OSPF and BGP details to 4.7–4.9.

chapters.idea: Distance vector routing has each router tell neighbours its distance vector, and Bellman-Ford updates pick the smallest neighbour cost plus link cost; RIP uses hop count.
chapters.depth: Cover the update rule D(x,y) = minᵥ [c(x,v) + D(v,y)], table exchange, convergence, count-to-infinity, split horizon, poison reverse and hold-down. Cover RIP hop count, maximum 15, 16 as infinity, 30-second updates and RIPv2. Some syllabi call this Bellman-Ford routing.

figure.aria: Routers A and B sit one hop apart; B's link to C is down, while A still has a stale route to C of cost 2 through B.

chapters.example: Routers A—B—C have link cost 1 each. C fails. Initially A has C=2 via B and B has C=1 via C. Give B and A values for the next two rounds and say when RIP declares infinity. Answer: B=3 via A, A=4 via B; next B=5, A=6; RIP treats 16 as infinity.
chapters.trap: RIP metric 16 is infinity, not a valid 16-hop route; count-to-infinity can still occur in loops even after simple fixes.

chapters.idea: Link state routing floods link-state packets so every router builds the same topology, then each runs Dijkstra to compute shortest paths; OSPF organises this into areas.
chapters.depth: Cover link-state packets, flooding, sequence numbers, aging, the topology database and Dijkstra's steps. Cover OSPF areas, backbone area 0, ABR and ASBR, DR and BDR, cost as reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, and LSA types at overview level. Some syllabi call this shortest path first routing.

figure.aria: Dijkstra from A gives B=1, C=3 via B, D=4 via C on the graph with edges A-B 1, A-C 4, B-C 2, B-D 5, C-D 1.

chapters.example: Run Dijkstra from A on the graph A-B 1, A-C 4, B-C 2, B-D 5, C-D 1. Give each node's shortest cost and the shortest path tree. Answer: B=1 via A; C=3 via B; D=4 via C; tree edges A-B, B-C, C-D.
chapters.trap: Using Dijkstra with negative weights; OSPF cost is not hop count; forgetting that all areas must connect to area 0.
chapters.leave: BGP to 4.9; multicast routing outside this book.

chapters.idea: Path vector routing exchanges full AS paths between autonomous systems; BGP uses these paths for loop detection and policy-based route choice.
chapters.depth: Cover eBGP and iBGP, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MED, origin and weight, and the main route-selection order. Explain policy, peering and transit at overview level. Some syllabi call this interdomain routing. Keep interior OSPF details in 4.8.

figure.aria: AS10 sees the prefix through AS20 with path [20,30] and through AS40 with path [40,50,60]; the first is shorter by AS count.

chapters.example: AS 10 learns 203.0.113.0/24 from AS 20 with path [20,30] and from AS 40 with path [40,50,60]. Which path wins by default? If LOCAL_PREF 200 is set for the AS 40 path, which wins? Answer: default shorter path [20,30]; with LOCAL_PREF 200, the AS 40 path wins because local preference is compared before AS path length.
chapters.trap: Assuming shortest AS path always wins; LOCAL_PREF and other attributes are compared first, and AS path length is only one tie-breaker.
chapters.leave: Multicast routing (MOSPF, DVMRP) and broadcast routing are outside this unit; a few universities add them.
